claims.text: In non-Nb–Ta-dominated high-entropy alloys, Tc is primarily governed by average valence electron count.
Average VEC tunes electron–phonon coupling strength and the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The starting material is a disordered solid solution containing at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
The proposed titanium-rich/heavy-transition-metal starting alloy is a single BCC or FCC phase without strong ordering.
Elemental substitutions can vary average VEC while leaving the solid-solution phase and crystallography unaltered.
Using identical pressure, temperature, and cooling rate ensures that only VEC is varied across the samples.
Random HEA lattices possess local lattice distortions caused by atomic-size differences.
The random, locally distorted lattice mediates the effect of VEC on the electronic environment.
Increasing average VEC increases the density of states at the Fermi level and strengthens electron–phonon coupling.
Stronger electron–phonon coupling caused by increased VEC raises Tc.
Decreasing average VEC weakens electron–phonon coupling and lowers Tc.
Samples with increased VEC should have higher Tc than the baseline, whereas samples with decreased VEC should have lower Tc, provided the phase is unchanged.
The baseline alloy's Tc is determined by its electron–phonon coupling strength and density of states.
The hypothesis applies only while the alloy remains a single disordered BCC or FCC solid-solution phase with minimal phase separation and confounding disorder effects.
Ordering, phase segregation, or sufficiently strong extrinsic disorder can overwhelm the proposed VEC effect.
The quantitative relationship between VEC changes and Tc changes is not established for these complex alloys.
Lattice distortion, local strain, and residual disorder may also affect superconductivity.
A lack of systematic directional variation of Tc with VEC, or a stronger correlation with structural or morphological changes, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention changes constituent elemental identities, but the conditions claim that only VEC is varied. Elemental substitution necessarily also changes chemical identity and may change atomic size, mass, bonding, disorder, and local strain, so identical processing does not by itself isolate VEC.
